title: The Flip: how sampling works - the breaks, the machines, the law and the money
description: An independent, cited guide to music sampling: the Amen break and the other most-sampled records, the SP-1200 and the MPC, the lawsuits from Biz Markie to Kraftwerk, how sample clearance works and what it costs, and what AI changes.

faq.a: Sampling is taking a piece of an existing recording and using it inside a new one. Re-recording the part instead is an interpolation, and re-recording the whole song is a cover.

A sample of a recording touches two copyrights, the recording and the song, and both owners can license or refuse it. US appeals courts disagree on whether a tiny sample can be too small to count, and the EU has its own rules on short samples and pastiche. This is general information, not legal advice.

faq.q: Is there a six-second rule for samples?
faq.a: No. The US Copyright Office calls the idea that seven seconds or less is always fair use fiction, and no court ruling sets a number of seconds below which a sample is free to use.

faq.q: What is the most sampled song of all time?
faq.a: "Amen, Brother" by The Winstons (1969), for its four-bar drum break. WhoSampled listed 6,873 uses as of July 2025.

faq.q: How much does it cost to clear a sample?
faq.a: There is no rate card. Each owner names a price, usually a fee up front plus a share of the new track, and either one is free to say no.

faq.q: What is the difference between a sample and an interpolation?
faq.a: A sample uses the original audio. An interpolation re-records the part, so it involves the owners of the song but not the owner of the original recording.
